articles.title: I Don't Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again
articles.body:
In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.
I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.
In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.
The Forensic Approach to Deepfake Detection
Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”
Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.
I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)
I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.
A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News
Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.
My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.
But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.
This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.
Signaling a Video’s Provenance
When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?
The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.
Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.
Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.
These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.
Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”
Real-Time Verification
This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.
In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.
All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.
This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.
Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today
Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to take shortcuts, such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.
Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the videoconferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be.
For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond what forensics alone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.
Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H. About 10 years ago, he randomly picked up a book in the library on the federal rules of evidence and was astonished to learn that courts made no distinction between photos from negatives and digital photos, even though the latter can be easily altered. “Digital photography was just getting started,” Farid says. “I realized this was really going to be a huge problem.” Since then digital photo forensics has become the focus of his research. He now frequently testifies in U.S. courts and advises law enforcement agencies. “All that from picking up a book,” he says.

articles.title: Andrey Zvyagintsev believes filmmakers know what the audience wants — not executives
articles.body:
The year is 2022. Vladimir Putin has announced the military draft. In Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur, set in the fictional town of Krasoborsk, a quietly unhappy couple, called Gleb and Galina, carry on with their lives, or try to, geopolitics notwithstanding. For Galina, carrying on means an affair, which we deduce from a scene of her texting with a faint smile, her face lit in the dark by the light of her phone. (Minotaur is a remake of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 film The Unfaithful Wife, whose title gives the plot away more readily than Zvyagintsev’s.)
Andrey Zvyagintsev believes filmmakers know what the audience wants — not executives
The director of Minotaur says there is no politics in Russia.
Meanwhile, Gleb runs a kind of private contracting concern and is soon asked to scare up military recruits to meet a quota. At this point, the domestic noir and the workplace drama merge to dramatic, devastating, and darkly funny effects.
In Minotaur, as in his five other features, Zvyagintsev has the camera moving seemingly objectively, almost omnisciently, putting the characters in their context. Occasionally they appear rather small, especially when set against the epic scale of their mythic and biblical fates. That the environment shapes the person seems to be a recurring revelation across all six of his staggering films. Minotaur, too, opens with a natural landscape of the arboreal kind and ends with another, different landscape, of clouds. In the middle is a movie about people trying to make sense of the landscapes they find themselves in, of the social, moral, relational variety.
Zvyagintsev has some experience with finding oneself in incomprehensible landscapes. After receiving Russia’s Sputnik V covid-19 vaccine during the pandemic, he fell ill, and later learned about the invasion of Ukraine while recovering from a medical coma in Germany. He subsequently chose not to return home, moving to France.
At the Cannes Film Festival in May, Minotaur won the second-highest honor. In his acceptance speech, Zvyagintsev spoke about the war, saying: “The only person who can stop this butchery is the President of the Russian Federation. Put an end to this carnage. The whole world is waiting for it.” While he resists the identity of exile, in September the Russian government designated him a “foreign agent.”
Zvyagintsev returned this year to the New York Film Festival, where he last visited with his 2014 film Leviathan, which won a Golden Globe and was nominated for an Oscar. His debut in 2003, The Return, won a top prize at Venice International Film Festival, after which he was invited to meet Putin, an account of which appears in his forthcoming book. Out of his six films, four have won prestigious prizes at Cannes, including Elena and Loveless.
We discussed the three years he spent cleaning the streets of Moscow in the early 1990s, his status as a Russian immigrant in France now, and how he captures that great Chekhovian instinct: that life is wretched, but what can we do, we must go on living. Zvyagintsev spoke to The Verge through a translator from Los Angeles.
I understand you went from cleaning streets to making commercials. What happened in between?
It kind of happened almost at the same time, because I was cleaning the streets to be able to live in Moscow. From 1990 to 1993, I was cleaning the streets. And then I was going to the Museum of Cinema and watching a movie every single day. Those were my formative years, when I learned a lot about cinema.
And then I was let go.
I had been living in a huge communal flat, free accommodation in a beautiful historic mansion in central Moscow. It was a really big apartment, and there were three street cleaners, including me, that lived there. In 1993, I was forced to leave the apartment after someone from the local housing administration decided to take it over. The two others had families, so they decided that if someone was supposed to move, it was going to be me, since I was single.
I was offered alternative accommodation, but realized that the only reason I had continued working as a street sweeper was to keep that particular apartment.
So the first night when I had to leave the apartment, I left it fast without an actual plan. I had to spend the night inside a truck that was abandoned and that was parked in the street.
I got a new job as a guard, as a night guard at a kindergarten where I also ate leftover food from the children’s meals.
After the first day, I called my friend who was working in commercials and doing music videos. I asked him to help with a job, because I was sure I was able to shoot commercials. After the first commercial, I met some producers who liked my work, and then I started shooting commercials on the regular and working as a freelance for some time. One of those commercials was noticed by a producer from a TV channel called REN TV, who was shooting a bunch of TV series at the time. His name was Dmitry Lesnevsky and he asked me whether I wanted to shoot movies, and I said it was my dream. And then Dmitry presented me with 15 scripts of choice, and I shot three episodes of a television series called The Black Room for this channel, each 25 minutes long.
How did you know this friend?
We were army friends. He was a close friend from the army. He was a cinema mechanic. He was starting movies for the soldiers when they were in the army. They had a theater, and I was in the music ensemble in the army. He was also an actor.
You had an adverse reaction to a covid vaccine. You were ill for a long time. You nearly died. You moved, and eventually settled in France. You’ve said you can’t know how that experience changed you as a filmmaker, but I’m curious if you know how that experience changed you as a person.
I got sick in Russia. I was in a coma for 40 days in Germany. I had a major problem with my lungs, a bacteria called klebsiella found its way there. They thought that they would need a lung transplant. Fortunately, the Germans were able to operate, and the transplant was not needed. I moved to France a year later after the coma.
What was the biggest change for me was the rhythm of life. I understood that you cannot lose time, so I’m trying to do things in a much more dynamic manner, and not leave things for later because we don’t know if this later exists. So that that’s the biggest change, really, just seeing life as something that passes by quickly.
You are a vocal opponent of the current Russian government. Do you consider yourself to be in political exile?
I am not in political exile. I did not have that status, and I never applied for it because I don’t see any necessity for that. I consider myself an immigrant. I’ve been living away from my native country for almost five years, but I did not leave on purpose. I was already in Europe when the war happened. There is a term in Russian, called nevozvrashchenets, which means a person who does not come back, someone who has left their home country and has not returned, particularly for political reasons. I was in the clinic in Germany and then in France when the war started, and I realized that I could not go back to the country that is at war.
You’ve said you are not political, but your movies seem overtly political, to me. You’ve also said that the job of an artist is to reflect reality. You don’t think you’re political, but your job is to reflect reality, and we are living at a time when politics is dominant. How do you reconcile all this?
It’s very simple to reconcile. It’s just that the politics barges into our lives, and we have to reflect what’s going on in the world. You become a witness of what’s going on beyond your window, what’s going on to the environment, to the world around you, to the world close to you. It just so happens that the politics dominate our lives. We are witnessing historical events that we cannot not reflect in the movies.
“There is no politics in Russia, in the sense of politics being a struggle for power, dialogue between different parties or worldviews… This does not exist in Russia. There’s only one power”
When I say I’m not a political animal, I mean that I have no way of influencing the political process in my country, especially while the war is going on. There is no politics in Russia, in the sense of politics being a struggle for power, dialogue between different parties or worldviews, you know, left, right, Democrats, Republicans. This does not exist in Russia. There’s only one power.
It feels more like domination in the way Foucault meant it.
Yes. It’s not even that there is only one party that dominates. It’s that no one even questions it, and no one even tries to struggle. It’s kind of a totalitarian regime at this time.
Let’s talk Minotaur. I believe you said you wanted to adapt Ingrid Bergman first, but when that didn’t go, you asked your producers for other available properties and they sent you a list. You also said you asked for marital dramas from the ’60s and ’70s specifically. Why?
I wanted to do a remake of a movie that would have three or four main characters, not a lot of different locations, that would be a little more compact, because there was a certain budget consideration. The films that I had previously considered, the scripts I considered, were more expensive, and so I was not able to get any of them going.
And that’s when I asked for the list from my friend who is French, and he gave me a list of French films. If I had an Italian friend, those would have been Italian movies.
I asked him for the best films from the ’60s and ’70s because it’s far away enough for us, those were probably the films that were a little bit more forgotten by the public, or a new generation of the public maybe hasn’t seen them. And that’s how I discovered Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife.
You also said that something about the Chabrol did not work for you, and that’s what gave you the inspiration to want to remake it.
I wouldn’t formulate it as something not working, but I would rather say that he made a kind of a formal choice when it comes to the office life of the main character. Chabrol concentrates more on the crime plot and the love triangle [than the office life], which is totally his right.
And I thought it was something that I would like to fill in. In 2022, the war was going on, and then in September they started the partial mobilization in Russia, and so this plot kind of just barged into our movie, and filled out that space that was empty previously.
Your movies are full of scenes Hollywood executives would ask to cut. I am thinking of the ending of Minotaur, with the clouds, or The Banishment, which ends with women collecting hay and they are singing. What is the effect of these moments in your movies?
It would be impossible to cut out those moments.
What are they doing in the movie?
When you say that Hollywood execs would probably like to cut that stuff out, the viewers, including viewers in Hollywood, really like the clouds [that Minotaur ends on], for example, and they even tell me that the sequence could have been longer. So I want to tell you that the execs do not know what the viewers want because when the viewer goes to the cinema, he kind of goes to sleep and then he watches a dream. And as long as this dream is aesthetically pleasing and harmonious and beautiful, that’s what the viewers should be watching, and no one should cut that out.
This is the key conflict between the producer and the creator. The producer does not trust the creator to know what the audience wants, but the creator knows. And so, if the producer is so sure of himself, he should write a script himself.
You published a book about the making of your third film, Elena. I understand you’re working on a second book. What can you tell us about this project? Will it include advice to young filmmakers?
The whole book, in a way, will be an advice to younger filmmakers, or people who love movies, because it will be a very detailed account of the six films that I have released so far, six conversations with one of the best cinema critics writing in Russian, Anton Dolin.
Would you ever work in another language apart from Russian or with Netflix?
Yes, I am open. In fact, I have a script in English. Two even.

articles.title: Combatting Adversarial Distillation
articles.body:
Combatting adversarial distillation
How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.
As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.
We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.
Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.
We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.
We’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.
Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.
The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.
Our models help users with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.
In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to users—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.
We started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.
After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.
Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.
We defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards.
Adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners.
We use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses.
Tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.
API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models. Our September disclosure described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning.
With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API drops the reasoning that followed it(opens in a new window). We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning.
When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services.
This work extends beyond our own platform. Our consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments.
Sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.
To measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss.
We also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well.
Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better.
We have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September report. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer.
In order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, we also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to new attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations.
Adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we briefed(opens in a new window) Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we reported disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We plan to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted.
We support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act. Stronger export controls can limit adversaries’ access to the hardware needed to train frontier models. Distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained. Both efforts help maintain a U.S. lead in frontier AI, giving developers more room to slow a release when they need time to test safeguards.
Supporting the safe proliferation of frontier capabilities is an important goal of our anti-distillation work. Our experience so far suggests several useful steps that other model developers and platforms can take:
- Protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models.
- Keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and consistent with applicable privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses.
- Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.
- Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.
We have previously also shared findings through the Frontier Model Forum(opens in a new window) and appropriate government information-sharing channels to help other developers strengthen their defenses while keeping the details attackers could exploit private. We’ll continue working with researchers, developers, and partners to share what we learn about emerging attacks and effective defenses.
As we make frontier AI broadly available, our defenses against adversarial distillation aim to reduce the risk that its capabilities are reproduced without adequate safeguards, supporting our mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence is deployed safely and benefits all of humanity.

                 draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs-08
Abstract
   This document describes Merkle Tree certificates, a new form of X.509
   certificates which integrate public logging of the certificate, in
   the style of Certificate Transparency.  The integrated design reduces
   logging overhead in the face of both shorter-lived certificates and
   large post-quantum signature algorithms, while still achieving
   comparable security properties to existing X.509 constructions and
   Certificate Transparency.  Merkle Tree certificates additionally
   admit an optional size optimization that avoids signatures
   altogether, at the cost of only applying to up-to-date relying
   parties and older certificates.

1.  Introduction
   In Public Key Infrastructures (PKIs) that use Certificate
   Transparency (CT) [RFC6962] for a public logging requirement, an
   authenticating party must present Signed Certificate Timestamps
   (SCTs) alongside certificates.  CT policies often require two or more
   SCTs per certificate [APPLE-CT] [CHROME-CT], each of which carries a
   signature.  These signatures are in addition to those in the
   certificate chain itself.
   Current signature schemes can use as few as 32 bytes per key and 64
   bytes per signature [RFC8032], but post-quantum replacements are much
   larger.  For example, ML-DSA-44 [FIPS204] uses 1,312 bytes per public
   key and 2,420 bytes per signature.  ML-DSA-65 uses 1,952 bytes per
   public key and 3,309 bytes per signature.  Even with a directly-
   trusted intermediate (Section 9.5 of
   [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids]), two SCTs and a leaf certificate
   signature add 7,260 bytes of authentication overhead with ML-DSA-44
   and 9,927 bytes with ML-DSA-65.
   This increased overhead additionally impacts CT logs themselves.
   Most of a log's costs scale with the total storage size of the log.
   Each log entry contains both a public key, and a signature from the
   CA.  With larger public keys and signatures, the size of each log
   entry will grow.
   Additionally, as PKIs transition to shorter-lived certificates
   [CABF-153] [CABF-SC081], the rate at which entries are added to the
   log will increase.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                   [Page 5]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   This document introduces Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs), a new form
   of X.509 certificate that integrates logging with certificate
   issuance.  Each CA maintains logs of everything it issues, signing
   views of its logs to assert it has issued the contents.  The CA
   signature is combined with cosignatures from other parties who verify
   correct operation and optionally mirror the logs.  These signatures,
   together with an inclusion proof for an individual entry, constitute
   a certificate.
   This achieves the following:
   *  Log entries do not scale with public key and signature sizes.
      Entries replace public keys with hashes and do not contain
      signatures, while preserving non-repudiability (Section 12.4).
   *  Long-expired entries can be revoked from relying parties in bulk
      (see Section 7.5).  This allows logging and monitoring
      infrastructure to scale by retention policies, not the lifetime of
      the log, even as certificate lifetimes decrease.
   *  After a processing delay, authenticating parties can obtain a
      second "landmark-relative" certificate for the same log entry.
      This second certificate is an optional size optimization that
      avoids the need for any signatures, assuming an up-to-date client
      that has some predistributed log information.
   Section 3 gives an overview of the system.  Section 4 describes a
   Merkle Tree primitive used by this system.  Section 5.2 describes the
   log structure.  Finally, Section 6 and Section 7 describe how to
   construct and consume a Merkle Tree certificate.
2.  Conventions and Definitions
   The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT",
   "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and
   "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in
   BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all
   capitals, as shown here.
   This document additionally uses the TLS presentation language defined
   in Section 3 of [RFC9846], as well as the notation defined in
   Section 2.1.1 of [RFC9162].  It extends the numeric types defined in
   Section 3.3 of [RFC9846] with a big-endian, 48-bit integer:
   uint8 uint48[6];

Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   U+ followed by four hexadecimal characters denotes a Unicode
   codepoint, to be encoded in UTF-8 [RFC3629]. 0x followed by two
   hexadecimal characters denotes a byte value in the 0-255 range.
   The _decimal representation_ of a non-negative integer is its base-
   ten representation, written with the ASCII digits 0 through 9 (U+0030
   through U+0039).  Zero is written as the single digit 0, and no other
   value is written with a leading 0.
   [start, end), where start <= end, denotes the half-open interval
   containing integers x such that start <= x < end.
   Given a non-negative integer n,
   *  LSB(n) refers to the least-significant bit of n's binary
      representation.  Equivalently, it is the remainder when n is
      divided by 2.
   *  BIT_WIDTH(n) refers to the smallest number of bits needed to
      represent n.  BIT_WIDTH(0) is zero.
   *  POPCOUNT(n) refers to the number of set bits in n's binary
      representation.
   *  BIT_CEIL(n) refers to the smallest power of 2 that is greater or
      equal to n.
   To _left-shift_ a non-negative integer n is to shift each bit in its
   binary representation to one upper position.  Equivalently, it is n
   times 2.  Given non-negative integers a and b, a << b refers to a
   left-shifted b times.
   To _right-shift_ a non-negative integer n is to shift each bit in its
   binary representation to one lower position, discarding the least-
   significant bit.  Equivalently, it is the floor of n divided by 2.
   Given non-negative integers a and b, a >> b refers to a right-shifted
   b times.
   Given two non-negative integers a and b, a & b refers to the non-
   negative integer such that each bit position is set if the
   corresponding bit is set in both a and b, and unset otherwise.  This
   is commonly referred to as the bitwise AND operator.
2.1.  Terminology and Roles
   This document discusses the following roles:
   Authenticating party:  The party that authenticates itself in the
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                   [Page 7]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
      protocol.  In TLS, this is the side sending the Certificate and
      CertificateVerify message.
   Certification authority (CA):  The service that issues certificates
      to the authenticating party, after performing some validation
      process on the certificate contents.
   Relying party:  The party to whom the authenticating party presents
      its identity.  In TLS, this is the side receiving the Certificate
      and CertificateVerify message.
   Monitor:  Parties who watch logs for certificates of interest,
      analogous to the role in Section 8.2 of [RFC9162].
   Issuance log:  A log, maintained by the CA, containing certification
      statements issued by that CA.  A CA operates some number of
      issuance logs, which together contain all statements issued by
      that CA.
   Cosigner:  A service that signs views of an issuance log, to assert
      correct operation and other properties about the entries.
   Additionally, there are several terms used throughout this document
   to describe this proposal.  This section provides an overview.  They
   will be further defined and discussed in detail throughout the
   document.
   Checkpoint:  A description of the complete state of the log at some
      time.
   Entry:  An individual element of the log, describing information
      which the CA has validated and certified.
   Subtree:  A smaller Merkle Tree over a portion of the log, defined by
      an interior node of some snapshot of the log.  Subtrees can be
      efficiently shown to be consistent with the whole log.
   Inclusion proof:  A sequence of hashes that efficiently proves some
      entry is contained in some checkpoint or subtree.
   Consistency proof:  A sequence of hashes that efficiently proves a
      checkpoint or subtree is contained within another checkpoint.
   Cosignature:  A signature from either the CA or other cosigner, over
      some checkpoint or subtree.
   Landmark:  One of a sequence of tree sizes, infrequently chosen and

Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
      used to calculate landmark subtrees for predistribution to relying
      parties.
   Landmark subtree:  One of the two (possibly empty) subtrees
      determined by an interval between two landmarks.  Predistributed
      and used as the basis for landmark-relative certificates.
   Standalone certificate:  A certificate containing an inclusion proof
      to some subtree, and several cosignatures over that subtree.
   Landmark-relative certificate:  An optimized certificate containing
      an inclusion proof to a landmark subtree.  The landmark subtree is
      assumed to be known to the relying party, rather than
      authenticated by cosignatures.
   Directly-signed certificate:  A certificate issued using the
      existing, non-MTC construction, where the TBSCertificate is passed
      directly to the private key's signing operation.
3.  Overview
   In Certificate Transparency, a CA first certifies information by
   signing it, then submits the resulting certificate (or
   precertificate) to logs for logging.  Merkle Tree Certificates invert
   this process: the CA certifies information by logging it, then
   submits the log to cosigners to verify log operation.  A certificate
   is assembled from the result and proves the information is in the
   CA's log.

   Merkle Tree Certificates are issued as follows.  Figure 1 depicts
   this process.
   1.  The authenticating party requests a certificate, e.g. over ACME

   2.  The CA validates each incoming issuance request, e.g. with ACME

   3.  The CA operates a series of append-only _issuance logs_

       a.  The CA adds a TBSCertificateLogEntry (Section 5.2.1,
           abbreviated "tbscert entries" in the diagram) to an issuance
           log, describing the information it is certifying.
       b.  The CA signs a _checkpoint_, which describes the current
           state of the log.  A signed checkpoint certifies that the CA
           issued _every_ entry in the Merkle Tree (Section 5.4).
       c.  The CA additionally signs _subtrees_ (Section 4) that
           together contain certificates added since the last checkpoint
           (Section 4.5).  This is an optimization to reduce inclusion
           proof sizes.  A signed subtree certifies that the CA has
           issued _every_ entry in the subtree.
   4.  The CA submits the new log state to _cosigners_. Cosigners
       validate the log is append-only and optionally provide additional
       services, such as mirroring its contents.  They cosign the CA's
       checkpoints and subtrees.
   5.  The CA now has enough information to construct a certificate and
       give it to the authenticating party.  A certificate contains:
       *  The TBSCertificate being certified
       *  An inclusion proof from the TBSCertificate to some subtree
       *  Cosignatures from the CA and cosigners on the subtree
   6.  As in Certificate Transparency, monitors observe the CA's
       issuance logs to ensure the CA is operated correctly.
   A certificate with cosignatures is known as a _standalone
   certificate_. Analogous to X.509 trust anchors and trusted CT logs,
   relying parties are configured with trusted cosigners (Section 7.3)
   that allow them to accept Merkle Tree certificates.  The inclusion
   proof proves the TBSCertificate is part of some subtree, and
   cosignatures from trusted cosigners prove the subtree was certified
   by the CA and available to monitors.  Where CT logs entire
   certificates, the issuance log's entries are smaller
   TBSCertificateLogEntry (Section 5.2.1) structures, which do not scale
   with public key or signature size.
   This same issuance process also produces a _landmark-relative
   certificate_. This is an optional, optimized certificate that does
   not need subtree cosignatures, including any from the CA.  Landmark-
   relative certificates are available after a short period of time and
   usable with up-to-date relying parties.

4.  Subtrees
   This section extends the Merkle Tree definition in Section 2.1 of
   [RFC9162] by defining a _subtree_ of a Merkle Tree.  A subtree is
   itself a Merkle Tree, built over an interval of entries from the
   original tree.  Section 4.1 defines a subtree formally, including the
   constraints on those intervals.
   As with Merkle Trees, a subtree inclusion proof, defined in
   Section 4.3, can prove an entry is contained in some subtree.
   Subtrees, and thus their inclusion proofs, are smaller than those of
   the original tree, so this document uses subtree inclusion proofs as
   a certificate size optimization.
   Not all intervals can form subtrees.  Subtrees are limited to
   intervals that can be efficiently proven consistent with the original
   tree, using subtree consistency proofs defined in Section 4.4.
   However, every interval of a Merkle Tree can be efficiently covered
   by two subtrees.  Section 4.5 describes how to determine these
   subtrees.
   Appendix C.1 and Appendix C.2 provide test vectors for the algorithms
   defined in this section.
4.1.  Definition of a Subtree
   Given an ordered list of n inputs, D_n = {d[0], d[1], ..., d[n-1]},
   Section 2.1.1 of [RFC9162] defines the Merkle Tree via the Merkle
   Tree Hash MTH(D_n).
   A _subtree_ of this Merkle Tree is itself a Merkle Tree, defined by
   MTH(D[start:end]). start and end are integers such that:
   *  0 <= start <= end <= n
   *  start is a multiple of BIT_CEIL(end - start)
   The second condition ensures that MTH(D[start:end]), built over
   D[start:end] as an independent list, is sufficiently aligned with the
   original Merkle Tree to support subtree consistency proofs.  See
   Appendix B.2 for more details.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 13]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   In implementations using fixed-width integers, BIT_CEIL(end - start)
   above may exceed end and potentially overflow.  For example, if start
   is zero and end is 2^63+1, BIT_CEIL(end - start) is 2^64.  The
   following is an example C++ implementation that handles this
   condition.
   bool is_valid_subtree(uint64_t start, uint64_t end) {
     if (start > end) {
       return false;
     }
     uint64_t size = end - start;
     if (size > (uint64_t{1} << 63)) {
       return start == 0;  // bit_ceil below will overflow.
     }
     return (start & (std::bit_ceil(size) - 1)) == 0;
   }
   For all x, [0, x) is a valid subtree (0 is a multiple of everything),
   and [x, x) is a valid subtree (BIT_CEIL(0) is 1).
   The _size_ of the subtree is end - start.
   In the context of a single Merkle Tree, this document denotes subtree
   MTH(D[start:end]) by half-open interval [start, end).  It contains
   the entries whose indices are in that half-open interval.
   As a Merkle Tree grows, its subtrees remain unchanged.  That is, if
   end <= m <= n, the subtree [start, end) of MTH(D[0:m]) and the
   subtree [start, end) of MTH(D_n) are both valid and identical.

4.3.  Subtree Inclusion Proofs
   Subtrees are Merkle Trees, so entries can be proven to be contained
   in the subtree.  A subtree inclusion proof for entry index of the
   subtree [start, end) is a Merkle inclusion proof, as defined in
   Section 2.1.3.1 of [RFC9162], where m is index - start and the tree
   inputs are D[start:end].
   Subtree inclusion proofs contain a sequence of nodes that are
   sufficient to reconstruct the subtree hash, MTH(D[start:end]), out of
   the hash for entry index, MTH({d[index]}), thus demonstrating that
   the subtree hash contains the entry's hash.
   A subtree inclusion proof for a subtree of size n contains at most
   ceil(log2(n)) hashes, or BIT_WIDTH(n - 1) hashes.

4.3.2.  Evaluating a Subtree Inclusion Proof
   Given a subtree inclusion proof, inclusion_proof, for entry index,
   with hash entry_hash, of a subtree [start, end), the subtree
   inclusion proof can be _evaluated_ to compute the expected subtree
   hash:
   1.  Check that [start, end) is a valid subtree (Section 4.1), and
       that start <= index < end.  If either does not hold, fail proof
       evaluation.
   2.  Set fn to index - start and sn to end - start - 1.
   3.  Set r to entry_hash.
   4.  For each value p in the inclusion_proof array:
       1.  If sn is 0, then stop the iteration and fail proof
           evaluation.
       2.  If LSB(fn) is set, or if fn is equal to sn, then:
           1.  Set r to HASH(0x01 || p || r).
           2.  Until LSB(fn) is set, right-shift fn and sn equally.
           Otherwise:
           1.  Set r to HASH(0x01 || r || p).
       3.  Finally, right-shift both fn and sn one time.
   5.  If sn is not zero, fail proof evaluation.
   6.  Return r as the expected subtree hash.
   This is the same as the procedure in Section 2.1.3.2 of [RFC9162],
   where leaf_index is index - start, tree_size is end - start, and r is
   returned instead of compared with root_hash.
   Appendix B.3 explains this procedure in more detail.
4.3.3.  Verifying a Subtree Inclusion Proof
   Given a subtree inclusion proof, inclusion_proof, for entry index,
   with hash entry_hash, of a subtree [start, end) with hash
   subtree_hash, the subtree inclusion proof can be _verified_ to verify
   the described entry is contained in the subtree:
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 18]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   1.  Let expected_subtree_hash be the result of evaluating the
       inclusion proof as described Section 4.3.2.  If evaluation fails,
       fail the proof verification.
   2.  If subtree_hash is equal to expected_subtree_hash, the entry is
       contained in the subtree.  Otherwise, fail the proof
       verification.
4.4.  Subtree Consistency Proofs
   A subtree [start, end) can be efficiently proven to be consistent
   with the full Merkle Tree.  That is, given MTH(D[start:end]) and
   MTH(D_n), the proof demonstrates that the input D[start:end] to the
   subtree hash was equal to the corresponding elements of the input D_n
   to the Merkle Tree hash.
   Subtree consistency proofs contain sufficient nodes to reconstruct
   both the subtree hash, MTH(D[start:end]), and the original tree hash,
   MTH(D_n), in such a way that every input to the subtree hash was also
   incorporated into the original tree hash.
4.4.1.  Generating a Subtree Consistency Proof
   The subtree consistency proof, SUBTREE_PROOF(start, end, D_n) is
   defined similarly to Section 2.1.4.1 of [RFC9162].
   If start = end, the consistency proof is empty:
   SUBTREE_PROOF(start, start, D_n) = {}
   Otherwise, start < end and SUBTREE_PROOF is defined by a helper
   function:
   SUBTREE_PROOF(start, end, D_n) =
       SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(start, end, D_n, true)
   The boolean parameter tracks whether the first hash in the proof will
   be omitted by the base case.  The first hash is omitted when it's
   equal to the original subtree hash MTH(D[start:end]), since the
   verifier will already know that hash.  That happens when the original
   subtree's root is a node in the Merkle Tree constructed from D_n, or
   equivalently, when the original subtree is full or has end = n.
   If start = 0 and end = n, the subtree is the root (base case):
   SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(0, n, D_n, true) = {}
   SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(0, n, D_n, false) = {MTH(D_n)}
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 19]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   Otherwise, n > 1.  Let k be the largest power of two smaller than n.
   The consistency proof is defined recursively as:
   *  If end <= k, the subtree is on the left of k.  The proof proves
      consistency with the left child and includes the right child:
      SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(start, end, D_n, b) =
          SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(start, end, D[0:k], b) : MTH(D[k:n])
   *  If k <= start, the subtree is on the right of k.  The proof proves
      consistency with the right child and includes the left child.
      SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(start, end, D_n, b) =
          SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(start - k, end - k, D[k:n], b) : MTH(D[0:k])
   *  Otherwise, start < k < end, which implies start = 0.  The proof
      proves consistency with the right child and includes the left
      child.
      SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(0, end, D_n, b) =
          SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(0, end - k, D[k:n], false) : MTH(D[0:k])
   When start is zero, this computes a Merkle consistency proof:
   SUBTREE_PROOF(0, end, D_n) = PROOF(end, D_n)
   When end = start + 1, this computes a Merkle inclusion proof:
   SUBTREE_PROOF(start, start + 1, D_n) = PATH(start, D_n)
   Appendix B.4 explains the structure of a subtree consistency proof in
   more detail.

4.4.3.  Verifying a Subtree Consistency Proof
   The following procedure can be used to verify a subtree consistency
   proof.
   Given a Merkle Tree over n elements, a subtree defined by [start,
   end), a consistency proof proof, a subtree hash node_hash, and a root
   hash root_hash:
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 22]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   1.  Check that [start, end) is a valid subtree (Section 4.1), and
       that end <= n.  If either does not hold, fail proof verification.
       These checks imply 0 <= start <= end <= n.
   2.  If start equals end, check the following conditions:
       *  proof is an empty array.
       *  node_hash is equal to HASH(), the hash of the empty string.
       If either condition does not hold, stop and fail the proof
       verification.  If both hold, stop and accept the proof.
   3.  Set fn to start, sn to end - 1, and tn to n - 1.
   4.  If sn is tn, then:
       1.  Until fn is sn, right-shift fn, sn, and tn equally.
   5.  Otherwise:
       1.  Until fn is sn or LSB(sn) is not set, right-shift fn, sn, and
           tn equally.
   6.  If fn is sn, set fr and sr to node_hash.
   7.  Otherwise:
       1.  If proof is an empty array, stop and fail verification.
       2.  Remove the first value of the proof array and set fr and sr
           to the removed value.
   8.  For each value c in the proof array:
       1.  If tn is 0, then stop the iteration and fail the proof
           verification.
       2.  If LSB(sn) is set, or if sn is equal to tn, then:
           1.  If fn < sn, set fr to HASH(0x01 || c || fr).
           2.  Set sr to HASH(0x01 || c || sr).
           3.  Until LSB(sn) is set, right-shift fn, sn, and tn equally.
       3.  Otherwise:
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 23]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
           1.  Set sr to HASH(0x01 || sr || c).
       4.  Right-shift fn, sn, and tn once more.
   9.  Compare tn to 0, fr to node_hash, and sr to root_hash.  If any
       are not equal, fail the proof verification.  If all are equal,
       accept the proof.
   Appendix B.5 explains this procedure in more detail.
4.5.  Efficiently Covering Arbitrary Intervals
   This document uses subtrees to sign over arbitrary intervals, [start,
   end), of a Merkle Tree.  However, not all intervals are valid
   subtrees.  While a protocol could build a smaller Merkle Tree,
   MTH(D[start:end]), and compute inclusion proofs of any element, this
   smaller Merkle Tree cannot, in general, be efficiently proven
   consistent with the overall Merkle Tree.
   Enlarging the interval to a valid subtree would mitigate this.
   However, the smallest subtree containing [start, end) may be much
   larger than [start, end).  For example, Figure 9 shows the smallest

4.5.1.  Selecting Two Subtrees
   Given any interval, [start, end), this section defines a procedure
   for selecting two subtrees, left and right, such that:
   *  left and right are valid subtrees, so it is possible to compute
      subtree consistency proofs.
   *  The disjoint union of left, followed by right, contains [start,
      end).  That is, left.start <= start <= left.end = right.start <=
      end <= right.end.
   *  While left may contain extra elements before start, right does not
      contain any extra elements.  That is, end = right.end.
   *  Each subtree's size is at most BIT_CEIL(end - start).
   The pair of subtree hashes for left and right can support inclusion
   proofs for any element of [start, end).  The largest such inclusion
   proof is no bigger than the largest inclusion proof in
   MTH(D[start:end]).  Unlike MTH(D[start:end]), these subtree hashes
   can be shown consistent with the overall Merkle Tree using subtree
   consistency proofs.
   The subtrees are selected as follows:
   1.  If end - start is less than or equal to 1, return the subtrees
       [start, end) and [end, end).
   2.  Otherwise:
       1.  Let last be end - 1, the last index in [start, end).
       2.  Let split be the bit index of the most significant bit where
           start and last differ.  Bits are numbered from the least
           significant bit, starting at zero. split is the height at
           which start and last's paths in the tree diverge.
       3.  Let mid be last with the least significant split bits set to
           zero. mid is the leftmost leaf node in the above divergence
           point's right branch.
       4.  Within the least significant split bits of start, let b be
           the bit index of the most significant bit with value zero, if
           any:
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 25]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
           1.  If there is such a bit, let left_split be b + 1.
           2.  Otherwise, let left_split be zero.
           left_split is the height of the lowest common ancestor of the
           nodes in [start, mid).
       5.  Let left_start be start with the least significant left_split
           bits set to zero. left_start is the above lowest common
           ancestor's leftmost leaf node.
       6.  Return the subtrees [left_start, mid) and [mid, end).
   Intuitively, this procedure considers the tree MTH(D[0:end]) and
   finds the lowest common ancestor of the elements in [start, end).  It
   splits the interval by that ancestor's left and right children and
   returns the lowest common ancestor of each half.
   The following Python code implements this procedure:
   def find_subtrees(start, end):
       """ Returns a pair of subtrees that efficiently cover
       [start, end). """
       assert start <= end
       if end - start <= 1:
           return (start, end), (end, end)
       last = end - 1
       # Find where start and last's tree paths diverge. The two
       # subtrees will be on either side of the split.
       split = (start ^ last).bit_length() - 1
       mask = (1 << split) - 1
       mid = last & ~mask
       # Maximize the left endpoint. This is just before start's
       # path leaves the right edge of its new subtree.
       left_split = (~start & mask).bit_length()
       left_start = start & ~((1 << left_split) - 1)
       return (left_start, mid), (mid, end)

5.  Certification Authorities
   A CA consists of the following components:
   *  A CA ID (Section 5.1), which uniquely identifies the CA.
   *  A collision-resistant cryptographic hash function, used by the
      CA's issuance logs.  SHA-256 [SHS] is RECOMMENDED.  Throughout
      this document, this hash function is referred to as HASH, and the
      size of its output in bytes is referred to as HASH_SIZE.
   *  A series of issuance logs (Section 5.2), which contain all
      statements the CA has certified.  One issuance log is designated
      as the current log.
   *  A CA cosigner (Section 5.4), which signs subtrees of issuance logs
      to certify their contents.
   *  Optionally, a landmark sequence per log (Section 6.4.1), to
      support optimized landmark-relative certificates.
   Section 5.5 defines an X.509 certificate representation of a CA.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 27]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
5.1.  Certification Authority Identifiers
   Each Merkle Tree Certificate CA has a _CA ID_ to identify it.  This
   CA ID is a trust anchor ID [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids].
   Once allocated, the ID's entire object identifier (OID) arc is
   reserved by this protocol.  Given a CA ID whose OID representation is
   caID, this document allocates the following OIDs:
   *  For each positive integer N, the OID {caID logs(0) N} represents
      the issuance log N (Section 5.2).
   *  For each positive integer N and L, the OID {caID landmarks(1) N L}
      represents landmark L (Section 6.4.1) of issuance log N.  These
      OIDs may be used as trust anchor IDs, as described in Section 8.2.
      These OIDs are used when it is necessary to identify an individual
      landmark, e.g. as in the recovery mechanism described in
      Section 5.6 of [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids].
   *  For each positive integer N and L, the OID {caID landmarkGroups(2)
      N L} represents a trust anchor group (Section 6 of
      [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids]) containing landmark L of log N
      and earlier landmarks of that log, as defined in Section 8.2.1.
      These OIDs may be used to advertise a series of landmarks at once.
   Future extensions to this protocol MAY define further allocations by
   adding to the registry defined in Section 13.2.3.
   The CA's ID determine's the CA's PKIX distinguished name using the
   construction described in Section 4.1 of
   [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids].
5.2.  Issuance Logs
   A CA operates a series of issuance logs, each identified by a
   positive integer _log number_. Log numbers are numbered consecutively
   from 1 to at most 65535 (2^16-1).
   Each issuance log has a _log ID_, which is a trust anchor ID
   constructed by concatenating the following OID components:
   *  The CA ID (Section 5.1)
   *  The constant 0
   *  The log number of the log
   A log ID specifies both the CA and the log number in a single ID.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 28]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   Each issuance log describes an append-only sequence of at most 2^48-1
   _entries_ (Section 5.2.1).  Each entry is identified by an integer
   _index_, assigned consecutively starting from zero.  Each entry is an
   assertion that the CA has certified.  The entries in the issuance log
   are represented as a Merkle Tree, described in Section 2.1 of
   [RFC9162].
   Unlike [RFC6962] and [RFC9162], an issuance log does not have a
   public submission interface.  The log only contains entries which the
   log operator, i.e. the CA, chose to add.  As entries are added, the
   Merkle Tree is updated to be computed over the new sequence.
   A snapshot of the log is known as a _checkpoint_. A checkpoint is
   identified by its _tree size_, that is the number of elements
   committed to the log at the time.  Its contents can be described by
   the Merkle Tree Hash (Section 2.1.1 of [RFC9162]) of entries zero
   through tree_size - 1.
   At any point in time, one of the CA's issuance logs is its _current_
   log.  Initially, this is log 1.  A CA MUST NOT append to any log that
   is not the current log.  Logs before the current log may have
   historical entries.  Logs after the current log MUST be empty.  A CA
   MAY increment its current log number as part of recovering from
   certain operational failures.  See Section 12.2.1 for further
   discussion.
5.2.1.  Log Entries
   Each entry in the log is an MTCLogEntry, defined with the TLS
   presentation syntax below.  An MTCLogEntry describes certificate
   information that the CA has validated and certified.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 29]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   struct {} Empty;
   enum { (2^16-1) } MTCLogEntryExtensionType;
   struct {
       MTCLogEntryExtensionType extension_type;
       opaque extension_data<0..2^16-1>;
   } MTCLogEntryExtension;
   enum {
       null_entry(0), tbs_cert_entry(1), (2^16-1)
   } MTCLogEntryType;
   struct {
       MTCLogEntryExtension extensions<0..2^16-1>;
       MTCLogEntryType type;
       select (type) {
          case null_entry: Empty;
          case tbs_cert_entry: opaque tbs_cert_entry_data[N];
          /* May be extended with future types. */
       }

   associated with the log entry.  Extensions MUST appear in the list in
   ascending order by extension_type, and the list MUST NOT contain two
   extensions with the same extension_type.
   When type is null_entry, the entry does not represent any
   information.  Entries at any index in the log MAY have type
   null_entry.
   When type is tbs_cert_entry, N is the number of bytes needed to

5.2.2.  Publishing Logs
   This protocol aims to enable monitors to detect misissued
   certificates by observing the issuance log.  See Section 12.2.
   This document does not prescribe a particular method of observing the
   issuance log.  The access protocols do not affect certificate
   interoperability, and different applications could have different
   needs.  For example, a PKI that authenticates public services might
   publicly serve issuance logs, while a PKI that authenticates a single
   organization's intranet services might keep the log private to the
   organization.  Relying parties SHOULD define log serving
   requirements, including the allowed protocols and expected
   availability, as part of their policies on which CAs to support.  See
   also Section 10.3.
   If a serving protocol supports serving only a portion of the log,
   relying party policies SHOULD include requirements on which portions
   to serve.
   For example, [MTC-TLOG] defines a profile for Merkle Tree
   Certificates that uses [TLOG-TILES].
